facts.fact_text: The opposition group Ictimai Palata was planning a demonstration to be held on 19 June 2011 in Baku.
According to the notice, the assembly was scheduled to take place from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. on 19 June 2011 at the square in front of the Narimanov Cinema in Baku.
According to the applicant, the demonstration was intended to be peaceful.
According to the applicant, the demonstration was conducted in a peaceful manner.
The applicant attended the demonstration near the Puppet Theatre on Seaside Boulevard on 19 June 2011.
The Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) refused to authorise the holding of the demonstration at the place indicated by the organisers (the square in front of the Narimanov Cinema in Baku).
The Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) proposed another location on the outskirts of Baku as an alternative to the place indicated by the organisers.
Despite the Baku City Executive Authority's refusal, the organisers decided to hold the demonstration in one of the central areas of Baku, namely near the Puppet Theatre on Seaside Boulevard.
Shortly after the demonstration had started, the police started to disperse it.
The applicant was arrested at around 6.10 p.m. on 19 June 2011 during the dispersal operation.
The Sabail District Court convicted the applicant under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO).
The Sabail District Court sentenced the applicant to five days' administrative detention.

Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, advance written notification is required in order to agree upon the place and time of an assembly and upon the route of a march, with the purpose of enabling the relevant local executive authority to take necessary measures.
Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, the notification must be done in writing five days before the demonstration.

Article 8 §§ IV and V of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to prohibit a public assembly.
Article 8 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to stop a public assembly.

Article 9 §§ II and VII of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to restrict or change the place, route and/or time of a public assembly.
Article 9 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to designate specific areas for public assemblies.

At the material time, Article 14 § I(2) of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provided that police authorities have the power, when necessary, to stop an assembly which has not been notified to the authorities beforehand, save for spontaneous assemblies.

At the material time, Article 14 § II(2) of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provided that police authorities have the power to order the organisers and participants of an assembly to use all available opportunities to stop the assembly and to disperse, with regard to the execution of orders specified under Article 8 §§ V and VI of that Law.

At the material time, Article 14 § II(3) of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provided that police authorities have the power to warn organisers and participants that physical force or exceptional measures will be used against them if the order to stop the assembly and to disperse is not complied with.

At the material time, Article 14 § II(4) of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provided that police authorities have the power to use physical force or exceptional measures in order to stop an assembly and disperse participants, in accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

At the material time, Article 14 § II(5) of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provided that police authorities have the power to apprehend persons not complying with the order to stop an assembly and disperse.

At the material time, Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) of 2000 provided that deliberate failure by an individual to comply with the lawful order of a police officer or military serviceman carrying out their duties to protect public order shall be punishable by a fine of twenty to twenty-five manats (AZN) or, if that sanction is inadequate in the circumstances of the case and taking into account the character of the offender, by administrative detention for a term of up to fifteen days.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe noted that the organisers of protests in Baku in March and April 2011 were denied permission to demonstrate in a central square and other places in the city centre in Baku, and were instead authorised to hold a demonstration in the outskirts of the city.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, in document CommDH(2011)33 dated 29 September 2011, criticised the method of curbing the impact of a demonstration by allowing it to take place only at another time and at a less central location, thereby diminishing significantly the visibility of the rally and its message to the general public.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that while the Law on Freedom of Assembly is in line with international standards, undue restrictions of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly are widely reported in practice.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that the problems with freedom of assembly in Azerbaijan mainly stem from the interpretation of Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, which provides for a notification procedure before convening an assembly.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that the Azerbaijani authorities confirmed that the legislation does not require permission for rallies, but the authorities appear to have interpreted it as requiring such permission, and a system of authorisation has in practice replaced the system of notification.
The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that peaceful protesters have been effectively banned from demonstrating in central Baku since 2006, despite advanced notification of the assemblies.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that several requests by the political opposition or civil society to hold demonstrations were allegedly denied or, when allowed, organisers were obliged to have them in areas very remote from the city centre of Baku.

The Human Rights Watch Report 'Tightening the Screws: Azerbaijan's Crackdown on Civil Society and Dissent' (2013) noted that the Baku municipal authorities have implemented a blanket ban on all opposition demonstrations in the city center since early 2006.

The Human Rights Watch Report 'Tightening the Screws: Azerbaijan's Crackdown on Civil Society and Dissent' (2013) noted that while the constitution of Azerbaijan stipulates that groups may peacefully assemble after simply notifying the relevant government body in advance, in practice authorities require that gatherings obtain a permit issued by local municipalities.

The Human Rights Watch Report 'Tightening the Screws: Azerbaijan's Crackdown on Civil Society and Dissent' (2013) noted that municipal authorities have effectively banned all forms of peaceful protest from the center of Baku and instead force all demonstrations into designated zones on the outskirts of the city.

The Human Rights Watch Report 'Tightening the Screws: Azerbaijan's Crackdown on Civil Society and Dissent' (2013) stated that such a blanket ban on freedom of assembly in the central areas of Baku violates Azerbaijan's international obligations to respect freedom of assembly and expression.

Police officers Z.H. and J.M. submitted a report (raport) to a superior police officer stating that at around 6.10 p.m. they were on duty when Mammadov Gafgaz Suleyman oglu, whose identity was established later, was attempting to hold an unlawful demonstration.

The administrative-offence report stated that by deliberately failing to comply with the lawful order of the police during the demonstration, the applicant had committed an administrative offence under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO).
The Sabail District Court found that the applicant had failed to stop participating in the unauthorised demonstration.
The opposition group Ictimai Palata was planning a demonstration to be held on 19 June 2011 in Baku.
On 9 June 2011, the organisers of the demonstration — consisting of several members of Ictimai Palata — gave prior notice to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA).
The prior notice given to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) on 9 June 2011 informed it of the date, time, place and purpose of the demonstration.
According to the notice, the assembly was scheduled to take place from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. on 19 June 2011 at the square in front of the Narimanov Cinema in Baku.
The Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) refused to authorise the holding of the demonstration at the place indicated by the organisers (the square in front of the Narimanov Cinema in Baku).
The Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) proposed another location on the outskirts of Baku as an alternative to the place indicated by the organisers.
Despite the Baku City Executive Authority's refusal, the organisers decided to hold the demonstration in one of the central areas of Baku, namely near the Puppet Theatre on Seaside Boulevard.
According to the applicant, the demonstration was intended to be peaceful.
According to the applicant, the demonstration was conducted in a peaceful manner.
The participants of the demonstration were demanding free and fair elections.
The participants of the demonstration were demanding democratic reforms.
The participants of the demonstration were demanding freedom of assembly.
The participants of the demonstration were demanding the release of persons arrested during some previous demonstrations.
The applicant attended the demonstration near the Puppet Theatre on Seaside Boulevard on 19 June 2011.
Shortly after the demonstration had started, the police started to disperse it.
The applicant was arrested at around 6.10 p.m. on 19 June 2011 during the dispersal operation.
The applicant stated before the Sabail District Court that he was not guilty of disobeying a lawful order of a police officer.
The applicant stated before the Sabail District Court that he had participated in the demonstration because he had a constitutional right to freedom of assembly.
According to the record of the hearing provided by the Government, the applicant stated that the police's demand to disperse was not lawful because the demonstrators were exercising their right.

According to the record of the hearing provided by the Government, the applicant stated that instead of calling on the demonstrators to disperse, the responsibility of the police should have been to ensure their security.

Police officer Z.H. testified that at around 6.10 p.m. on 19 June 2011 he noticed that the applicant, together with a group of other people, was attempting to hold an unauthorised demonstration by shouting out slogans.
Police officer Z.H. testified that he asked the applicant and the group of people to observe silence.
Police officer Z.H. testified that the applicant continued his actions, disobeying the police officers' requests.
The Sabail District Court found that the applicant had failed to stop participating in the unauthorised demonstration.
The Sabail District Court convicted the applicant under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO).
The Sabail District Court sentenced the applicant to five days' administrative detention.
The applicant lodged an appeal before the Baku Court of Appeal arguing that his conviction was in violation of his rights because the demonstration in which he had participated had been peaceful.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that the most frequent problems encountered in Azerbaijan include the banning of demonstrations in central and easily accessible locations and the use of force to disperse demonstrations which still go ahead, leading to arrests and, in some cases, harsh sentences.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that while the Law on Freedom of Assembly is in line with international standards, undue restrictions of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly are widely reported in practice.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that the Azerbaijani authorities confirmed that the legislation does not require permission for rallies, but the authorities appear to have interpreted it as requiring such permission, and a system of authorisation has in practice replaced the system of notification.
The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that peaceful protesters have been effectively banned from demonstrating in central Baku since 2006, despite advanced notification of the assemblies.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 noted that several requests by the political opposition or civil society to hold demonstrations were allegedly denied or, when allowed, organisers were obliged to have them in areas very remote from the city centre of Baku.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 stated that the authorities should seek to facilitate and protect public assemblies at the organisers' preferred location, given the need for tolerance in a democratic society.

The Report CommDH(2013)14 stated that participants in peaceful assemblies should not be sanctioned for the mere fact of being present at and actively participating in the demonstration in question, provided they do not do anything illegal, violent or obscene in the course of it.
